articles.title: What a wealth tax looks like in the age of AI billionaires
articles.summary: Anthropic’s initial public offering has created overnight multi-millionaires (and some billionaires), and the timing is complicated.
articles.body:
Anthropic's initial public offering has created overnight multi-millionaires (and some billionaires), and the timing is complicated.

They are coming into incredible wealth just as some states are trying different forms of wealth taxes, fueled by a shrinking middle class and growing unease about the concentration of wealth and power.

New York City is about to charge an extra yearly tax on expensive homes that aren't anyone's primary residence. Washington, DC is considering a tax on investment income for wealthier households. Washington state will levy its first modern income tax on households making more than $1 million in 2028.

California's Prop 40 "billionaire tax" failed on Election Day, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D- MD) told Politico that the failure of Prop 40 suggests one state can't do it alone . A bill introduced in both the House and Senate already proposes a 5% tax on the net worth of America's billionaires, which could become a flashpoint in the 2028 presidential election.

Prop 40's defeat — and the sudden emergence of a new class of AI elite — has simply launched a more heated national debate about how exactly the rich should be taxed.

"If someone's worth $1 billion, that doesn't mean that they have $50 million of cash around to pay the tax," said Anderson Lafontant, managing director of Blue Zone Wealth Advisors.

Lafontant, whose clients include employees of AI companies, said a lot of this net worth is mostly on paper. Companies in IPO scenarios have restrictions on when shareholders can sell stock after it goes public, so an employee may not hold much liquid cash until their shares are sold. (Lafontant does not currently work with any Anthropic employees or founders.)

Prop 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who lived in California on January 1, 2026, not counting real estate or most retirement accounts.

"That's the point about a wealth tax, is it hits paper wealth," said Tom Steyer, billionaire climate activist and former California gubernatorial candidate. He argues that a person could borrow against stock to pay taxes. He called Prop 40 "imperfect" but "better than nothing."

Megan Lisa Jones, a private wealth and tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said some of her clients have left or talked about leaving California to seek better tax rates and avoid a potential Prop 40. Lafontant also said some of her clients have moved for tax reasons, though not necessarily over a wealth tax.

articles.title: ‘It’s greed’: Zohran Mamdani blasts Amazon over new $5 fee hike in NYC. Is your next order about to get pricier?
articles.summary: An express delivery straight against your bottom line.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is taking aim at Amazon over a warning the online retail giant has been flashing at New Yorkers as they shop: Their orders could soon cost as much as $5 more.

"Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe," Mamdani wrote in a Nov. 19 post on X (1). "It's greed."

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 5 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

Amazon is fighting a proposed New York City law (2) that would overhaul how the company gets packages from its warehouses to your doorstep. And now the giant seems to be recruiting its own customers to help fight that legislative battle.

The company has begun displaying warnings on its website and in its shopping app, directing customers to contact their local lawmakers and oppose the legislation.

For Americans who have come to depend on the convenience of online shopping, the prospect of paying more every time they click "buy" is hardly welcome news. But how much of Amazon's warning should shoppers take at face value?

Why Amazon is threatening to raise prices

Introduced in February by New York City Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán, the Delivery Protection Act (3) would require companies operating certain delivery facilities to directly employ most of their warehouse and delivery workers rather than outsource those jobs to third-party contractors.

The legislation would also establish a $500 annual licensing fee per facility, mandatory worker safety training and additional protections against unfair dismissal.

Amazon contends that complying with the legislation could make its existing delivery model economically untenable in New York City, potentially forcing it to relocate operations beyond city limits.

The company has cited research from consulting firm AKRF estimating additional annual household costs of between $409 and $664. However, Amazon hasn't established precisely how those figures translate into a $5 increase per order, per Fox Business (4).

And the bill, which remains in committee, hasn't passed yet.

articles.title: What really happens when you need help restoring your identity
articles.summary: Identity theft restoration involves credit freezes, fraud alerts and disputing fraudulent records. Here's how the recovery process works, step by step.
articles.body: Identity theft restoration takes more than one phone call. It often means securing accounts, documenting fraudulent activity and working with several companies to correct inaccurate records. The term "identity restoration" can sound complicated until you suddenly need it. Maybe someone opened a credit card in your name, took over your bank account or used your personal information to get medical care. Now you're dealing with unfamiliar charges, paperwork and companies that all seem to have different requirements. Fortunately, knowing what happens during recovery can make the process easier to manage. Here's how identity restoration typically works, what you may need to do yourself and where professional help can make a difference. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT 1. The first conversation establishes what happened Identity restoration usually starts with understanding the problem. A specialist may ask when you first noticed suspicious activity, which accounts someone accessed and whether you lost money or personal information. These details help identify the type of identity theft involved. Someone opening a credit card in your name requires a different response than a criminal taking over your phone number or using your medical information. A restoration specialist can help you separate confirmed fraud from suspicious activity that still needs investigation. As a result, you can focus on the companies and accounts that need attention first. 2. The immediate risk gets contained Before tackling paperwork, focus on preventing additional damage. Depending on what happened, you may need to contact your bank, lock a credit card, change passwords or secure your mobile phone account. If someone accessed your email, make securing that account an early priority. Criminals can use compromised email accounts to reset passwords and gain access to other services. You may also want to place a fraud alert or freeze your credit. Neither option fixes fraud that has already occurred. However, both can help reduce the risk of additional new-account fraud. 3. A case file helps keep everything organized One of the most frustrating parts of identity theft recovery is having to explain the same problem repeatedly. A case file helps you keep track of important information and avoid starting over with every phone call. Include dates of suspicious activity, copies of statements, confirmation numbers, correspondence and the names of representatives you've contacted. Also, record what each company promised to do and when you should expect a response. This becomes especially helpful when several organizations are involved. For example, your bank might close an account while a fraudulent balance still appears on your credit report. Having documentation gives you a clear record of the steps you've already completed. Keep those records somewhere secure. Additionally, avoid sending sensitive documents through unverified email addresses or links. 4. The appropriate institutions get involved Depending on the type of fraud, identity restoration may involve banks, creditors, credit bureaus, mobile carriers, medical providers or government agencies. Each organization follows its own procedures. A bank may ask you to complete a fraud affidavit, while a credit bureau may request an identity theft report before blocking fraudulent information. A restoration specialist can explain those requirements and help you navigate the process. In some situations, the specialist may also coordinate communications or work with institutions on your behalf. However, you may still need to verify your identity, provide documents or authorize certain actions. Restoration assistance helps you work through the process, but the affected institutions remain responsible for reviewing claims and correcting their records. 5. You dispute and correct fraudulent records Once you secure your accounts and identify the affected organizations, the next step involves correcting the damage. If someone opened a fraudulent credit account, you may need to dispute the information with the creditor and the credit bureaus. The Federal Trade Commission recommends reporting identity theft through IdentityTheft.gov, where you can create an FTC Identity Theft Report and receive a personalized recovery plan. An FTC Identity Theft Report can also help you exercise important rights, including requesting that credit bureaus block information resulting from identity theft. Medical identity theft may require contacting healthcare providers and insurers to correct inaccurate records. Meanwhile, tax identity theft generally involves working directly with the IRS. Keep copies of every document you submit. Whenever possible, request written confirmation after an organization resolves an issue. 6. Follow-ups continue until the problems are resolved Identity theft recovery rarely happens all at once. Your bank might reverse a fraudulent transaction before a credit bureau finishes investigating a related account. Similarly, a phone carrier may restore your number, but you may still need to strengthen account security to prevent another takeover. That's why follow-ups are so important. Set reminders for promised responses and continue checking your statements, accounts and credit reports after the initial incident. You can review your credit reports for free each week at AnnualCreditReport.com. Even after you resolve a case, additional suspicious activity can surface if criminals continue trying to use your stolen information. WAS YOUR IDENTITY STOLEN? WHAT TO DO IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS Recovery depends on the type of identity theft Not every identity theft case follows the same path. The type of fraud determines which organizations need to get involved and what steps you should take. For example, new-account fraud often involves creditors and credit bureaus. An existing bank-account takeover requires immediate attention from the financial institution, while medical identity theft may involve correcting treatment and billing records. Tax or government benefits fraud can require separate reporting procedures. And if a scammer convinced you to authorize a payment, your options may differ from those available for unauthorized account transactions. That's why identifying the problem early is important. A credit freeze may help protect against new credit accounts, but it cannot correct a medical record or recover money sent to a scammer. How to tell whether your recovery is progressing Identity theft recovery can feel slow, especially when you're waiting for several companies to respond. However, you can track progress by focusing on specific actions rather than expecting everything to happen immediately. Have you secured the compromised account? Did you report the fraudulent charge? Has the credit bureau acknowledged your dispute? Each completed step helps move the case forward. If a company misses a deadline or provides conflicting information, your case file will help you explain the situation without starting the conversation from scratch. What you may need to provide during restoration Before speaking with a restoration specialist or fraud department, gather any suspicious statements, letters, alerts or emails connected to the incident. The company may also ask you to provide identification, an FTC Identity Theft Report or written authorization allowing someone to assist with your case. Always verify that you're communicating with the legitimate organization before sharing sensitive information. Also, ask why a document is necessary and how the company plans to handle it. Ultimately, you should understand what information you're providing and what actions someone may take on your behalf. How an identity protection service can help with restoration If you've experienced identity theft, handling multiple disputes and follow-up calls yourself can become overwhelming. That's where an identity protection service may help. Some services provide access to identity restoration specialists who can guide you through the recovery process. Depending on the provider and your plan, specialists may help organize documentation, explain next steps and assist with communications involving affected institutions. Identity protection services may also monitor certain personal information, credit reports and financial accounts. Alerts can help you discover suspicious activity before it leads to additional problems. However, identity monitoring cannot detect every form of fraud, and restoration assistance cannot guarantee that every dispute will end in your favor. The benefit comes from having experienced support when you're trying to work through a complicated situation. Other identity protection tools that can support recovery Beyond restoration assistance, some identity protection services offer tools that help you identify suspicious activity, reduce the exposure of personal information and respond when something looks wrong. Features vary by provider and plan, so it's worth checking what's included before signing up. Review where your payment card information is stored Some services offer tools that help you identify merchants and websites that may have your payment card information on file. Reviewing these connections can help you decide where to remove stored payment details, especially if you no longer use certain accounts. However, these tools cannot automatically confirm whether someone has stolen your card information. Unexpected and suspicious charge alerts Certain identity protection services can monitor eligible financial accounts and flag transactions that appear unusual or potentially fraudulent. These might include unfamiliar purchases or unexpected charges. An alert gives you an opportunity to review the transaction and contact your financial institution if necessary. Keep in mind that these services may not detect every suspicious transaction. Personal data removal services Some identity protection services include tools that search covered data broker websites for your personal information and submit removal requests on your behalf. Reducing publicly available information may help limit your exposure to identity theft and scams. However, no removal service can erase your information from every website or guarantee that it will never reappear. Scam assistance and identity protection guidance Some providers offer access to support specialists or online tools that can help you evaluate suspicious messages, websites and financial activity. Depending on the service, you may receive guidance on reporting scams, securing accounts and taking steps to recover from identity theft. Certain plans may also include reimbursement benefits for eligible losses or expenses, subject to coverage limits and exclusions. However, these services cannot guarantee that you'll recover money you sent to a scammer. Always review the terms before relying on a particular benefit. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com Kurt's key takeaways When someone steals your identity, discovering the fraud is often only the beginning. The real work comes afterward, when you're trying to secure accounts, correct records and get answers from companies handling different parts of the problem. I've always believed that knowing what to do next can make a stressful situation much easier to handle. Start by protecting the accounts you still control, document everything and use the free recovery tools available through the FTC. If you want additional help, an identity protection service with restoration specialists may help you navigate the recovery process and stay organized. No service can promise an instant fix, but having experienced support can make a difference when you're dealing with identity theft. articles.title: America is definitely rich enough to fix Social Security and Medicare. Here’s how.
articles.summary: This one, simple, low-pain tax solves all the problems.
articles.body:
To hear many people tell it, America's looming fiscal crises can't be fixed without enormous pain or costs — if it at all.

The country's national debt just hit $40 trillion, equal to about 100% of annual gross domestic product. Social Security's trust fund is due to run out of money in 2032 (or 2034 at the latest), and without some radical fix, benefits would have to be slashed by about a fifth. Medicare's Part A (hospital insurance) trust fund is due to run out of money around the same time. The trust fund for Medicare Part B (medical insurance) doesn't even have any money; it is funded by general tax revenues.

Any look at the long-term numbers seems terrifying: Trillions of dollars in deficits and unfunded liabilities, stretching as far as the eye can see.

Some say we will need to slash retirement benefits for future retirees, and drop millions from Medicaid (the latter is actually happening; it was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, along with tax cuts). Others talk about hefty income-tax hikes — for example, by abolishing the cap on the incomes subject to Social Security payroll taxes, which would effectively add an extra 12.4% tax on all income over $192,300 (in 2027).

Others offer big "wealth" taxes applied to the rich, the super-rich or the super-duper-rich. California voters just rejected a one-off 5% wealth tax on billionaires, but only after billionaires spent a fortune to defeat the measure. And the vote was pretty close.

But all of this is wrong. It is based on old-fashioned, outdated, backward-looking and increasingly irrelevant thinking, which is about as un-American as anything could be. It would be as if the U.S. government in the past had been supported by, say, a tax on buggy-whip sales, and as buggy whips passed into history, the revenues dried up, and the politicians and voters stood around, baffled, saying: "Well, we're screwed — there's nothing else we can do."

articles.title: Bessent warns on Fed hike as AI bubble fears mount
articles.summary: Traders have pared back expectations of a half-point hike on Dec. 9, after Anthropic’s record-setting IPO and a strong run of tech earnings failed to boost s...
articles.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Sunday that the Federal Reserve risks hurting the economy by overtightening policy , days after a tech-induced market correction intensified concerns that the AI bubble could be bursting.

Traders have pared back expectations of a half-point hike on Dec. 9, after Anthropic's record-setting IPO and a strong run of tech earnings failed to boost sentiment; some investors fear the Fed could be " tightening into an economic slowdown when both earnings and AI investment have peaked," an analyst told Reuters.

"Don't believe anyone who says the AI boom is different," a Bloomberg columnist argued, noting the busts that followed railroads, electrification, and the internet. " Be prepared for the tide to go out ."

articles.title: We haven’t seen the last of the major tech outages
articles.summary: Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.
articles.body: Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN: > “The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.” Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages on CBS News’ Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, but sounded a much more ominous tone. > “I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.” While the outages over the last week were not believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said. The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets. Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months. Update November 22nd: Added clarification that Smith was speaking on Face the Nation, not to CBS generally. Due to a typo, this article originally stated that the outages were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, the missing word has been corrected.

articles.title: Empresa deve pagar R$ 13,3 mil por cancelar passagens no RN | G1
articles.standfirst: Bilhetes seriam usados em viagem para um Campeonato Brasileiro no Rio de Janeiro, em 2021. Cancelamento ocorreu oito dias antes do embarque, e consumidores precisaram comprar novas passagens.
articles.summary: Justiça condenou fornecedora de passagens após cancelamento de sete bilhetes para campeonato de taekwondo oito dias antes da viagem.
articles.body:
A 2ª Vara da Comarca de Macau condenou uma empresa fornecedora de passagens aéreas a pagar R$ 13,3 mil a dois consumidores após o cancelamento de sete bilhetes que seriam usados por uma equipe de taekwondo em um Campeonato Brasileiro, no Rio de Janeiro, em novembro de 2021.

A sentença determinou o pagamento de R$ 3,3 mil por danos materiais e R$ 10 mil por danos morais. A indenização moral corresponde a R$ 5 mil para cada um dos autores do processo.

Segundo os autos, as sete passagens foram contratadas por R$ 7,7 mil e as reservas chegaram a ser disponibilizadas. Oito dias antes da viagem, no entanto, os bilhetes foram cancelados sem justificativa e o dinheiro não foi devolvido.

Com a proximidade da competição, a equipe precisou comprar novas passagens e buscar recursos de terceiros para conseguir viajar.

Na análise do processo, a juíza Brunna Melgaço Alves não reconheceu integralmente os R$ 7,7 mil apresentados pelos consumidores como prejuízo. Os comprovantes demonstraram quatro pagamentos, que somaram R$ 3,3 mil.

Um dos documentos apresentados correspondia a uma transferência já registrada em outro comprovante. Por isso, o valor foi contabilizado apenas uma vez.

A sentença aplicou o artigo 35 do Código de Defesa do Consumidor, que prevê a restituição do valor pago quando o fornecedor não cumpre a oferta. A magistrada não determinou a devolução em dobro, por entender que o caso envolveu o descumprimento do serviço contratado, e não uma cobrança indevida.

Ao avaliar os danos morais, a juíza considerou que o cancelamento ultrapassou um simples descumprimento contratual, já que ocorreu poucos dias antes de uma competição nacional previamente marcada e obrigou os consumidores a buscar alternativas para viabilizar a viagem.

A empresa também foi condenada a restituir os R$ 3,3 mil à autora que comprovou os pagamentos.

articles.title: Why Trump’s $350B defense push is losing steam on Capitol Hill
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s massive $350 billion defense reconciliation package is looking increasingly doomed in Congress, but the Pentagon hasn’t given up its push for a party-line bill. Key figures on both sides of the aisle are pessimistic about the chances of such a large package passing in the final weeks of the lame-duck session. The…
articles.body:
The Trump administration’s massive $350 billion defense reconciliation package is looking increasingly doomed in Congress, but the Pentagon hasn’t given up its push for a party-line bill.

Key figures on both sides of the aisle are pessimistic about the chances of such a large package passing in the final weeks of the lame-duck session. The administration views the request as a key pillar in President Trump’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget request.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Republicans sent their “most experienced appropriator” to negotiate with Democrats on “making a strong investment” in defense through the normal appropriations process.

“If that’s possible, perhaps reconciliation could be avoided,” Wicker told The Hill on Friday.

Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), who sits on the Armed Services Committee, said Thursday there are “some” holdouts on the $350 billion reconciliation package, which the Pentagon requested back in April, but lawmakers are having “family” discussions about a lower figure.

“Zero is the wrong number, right? So whatever number we can get through, yeah, it will be better than nothing,” Budd said in a brief interview.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), who chairs the key Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, said the military should be funded through regular appropriations.

“I’ll keep saying what I’ve said throughout the process: the way to show we’re serious about defense is to build new investments into sustainable, full-year appropriations,” McConnell said in a statement shared with The Hill.

“Reconciliation should have never been a substitute for finishing our work on FY27,” he added.

One source familiar with Capitol Hill discussions said Friday that the window for reconciliation had closed.

“Zero chance they get reconciliation done — any funding level,” the source said, placing the blame on the Pentagon for being “bad” at communicating the “why” behind the request.

“Choppy waters ahead for all defense things,” the source added.

Other Republicans said the Pentagon leadership did its job.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a Trump ally who sits on the Armed Services Committee, said Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have “always been accessible” and have kept him and the committee informed.

“Well, what I hope is, we get the entire 350 billion dollars. The military needs it. We have to understand that Communist China is trying to destroy us, kill us, and they are killing us with fentanyl,” Scott told The Hill on Friday. “This is a dangerous time for our country. And actually, the first thing we ought to be doing … is defending freedom of the country.”

The reconciliation request — which would allocate $48 billion for critical minerals; around $103 billion for low-cost autonomous systems, artificial intelligence and counter-unmanned systems; $47 billion for expanded munitions production; and $17 billion for the Golden Dome missile defense system — has been stalled for weeks on Capitol Hill over disagreements about how to pay for it. Some senators argue the Pentagon’s briefings have come too late in the game .

Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), the chair of the House Armed Services Committee, effectively declared the Pentagon’s top-line request dead last week.

“By the way, 350 is not going to happen. You may have guessed that, but a reconciliation bill is still possible. It’s going to have to be skinny down to deal with first and foremost the hole in the defense budget that Venezuela and Iran have created,” Rogers said Wednesday at a Hudson Institute event.

Rogers, who is not seeking a waiver to remain a top Republican on the House Armed Services Committee, said if the dollar amount can be trimmed down to $100 billion “or somewhere in that nature, there is a path for that.”

Reducing the request would mean shifting “essential” programs from the reconciliation bill into the baseline Pentagon budget request, set at $1.15 trillion, Rogers said.

Senate Democrats predict Republicans won’t move anything through reconciliation, and they say the Pentagon only has itself to blame for losing control of the defense budgeting process.

“I don’t think they’re going to get reconciliation at all,” Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the ranking member on the Senate Armed Services Committee, told The Hill on Friday. “They’re going to have to go through the budgetary process.”

“They deliberately refused to communicate with the full committee, Republican [and] Democrats. Didn’t forward reports required by law. Didn’t do anything that was consistent with law and custom. And then at the end, when they decided to make an approach, it was just the Republicans,” Reed said. “So they have mishandled the situation grotesquely.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who sits on the Armed Services Committee, said Thursday there will be cuts “because of opposition on both sides of the aisle.”

Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), who also sits on the committee, said she will let her Republican colleagues “speak for themselves,” but she criticized the U.S. war against Iran, which she said is “hurting everyone at the kitchen table.”

“We need to refill our stockpiles. We need to take care of our servicemen and women,” Rosen told The Hill on Friday. “So there’s a lot more important things to do than reconciliation.”

Sens. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), two other members of the Senate Armed Services Committee, announced Thursday that they will move to add an amendment to appropriations bills to block funding for offensive operations against Iran entirely.

Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly called on Congress to greenlight the $350 billion package, seeing it as an imperative defense spending hike that could be rammed through while Republicans control both chambers.

“I rebuilt our Military in my First Term, and we’re doing it AGAIN, bigger and better than ever before! The Radical Democrat Majority in the next Congress has already made it clear that their Number One Agenda is to BLOCK and RESIST this historic investment in our National Security,” the president wrote last week.

And the Pentagon, which has received bipartisan criticism over its lack of transparency , argued that it did its due diligence: briefing senators and staff to get everyone on the same page.

“No one can say this building isn’t putting in the legwork. Between senior leadership and the legislative affairs team, they are practically living on the Hill. We’ve briefed every single SASC office because we want zero daylight between our operational reality and what members see in the text,” a senior Pentagon official told The Hill.

Feinberg, a private equity billionaire, was on Capitol Hill all five days last week, briefing members on the $350 billion request and joining the Senate GOP lunch on Wednesday. The Hill also spotted Pentagon Comptroller Jules Hurst III on Friday leaving the Senate alongside Feinberg.

Senior Pentagon officials have conducted more than 45 individual meetings with senators and staff in the last two months, and the department is working with committee staff to figure out which “high-priority,” multiyear procurement programs — such as aircraft, munition contracts and Golden Dome sensing networks — could be shifted over to the base budget “if appropriators prefer that path,” the senior Pentagon official said.

Earlier this week, Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said during acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao’s confirmation hearing that there have been “multiple occasions” this year where his Democratic colleagues were not invited for classified briefings on defense programs, pointing out that it is difficult to build bipartisan support for the budget when they are not even present.

A second Pentagon official disagreed, saying, “We’ve made ourselves available, answered questions, and worked through concerns because we recognize how much is at stake for the men and women serving our country.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who has been fiercely critical of Pentagon leadership , indicated Thursday that if the administration can make a case for reconciliation that could pass through the House, he would jump on board. But he said Friday that he still has questions.

“I need some specific answers to square the math between a $350 billion replenishment request and an estimated $50 billion over the course of the war, right? How does that math work? So what is in there that is truly replenishment? Because that’s what we should go after first, and then build up other things that we may be willing to consider,” Tillis, who did not run for reelection, told reporters.

Dakota Meyer, Hegseth’s senior adviser who leads the Pentagon’s Barracks Task Force, said the reconciliation package would directly support the department’s mission to fix conditions at military installations and improve housing.

“Taking care of our people should never be about politics,” Meyer told The Hill on Friday. “The Senate has an opportunity to make a real difference in the lives of the men and women who signed up to serve our country. It’s time we serve them.”

articles.title: FBI warns AI hackers can breach systems in under 3 hours
articles.summary: The FBI warns the ARTEX AI hacking tool can give criminals privileged access in under three hours, targeting Microsoft 365 and financial firms.
articles.body: Your bank could spend millions protecting its computer systems. Your employer might have an entire cybersecurity team watching for suspicious activity. Yet hackers now have an AI-powered tool that can help them break into some organizations in less than three hours. The FBI is warning that criminals are using the ARTEX AI hacking tool to automate cyberattacks against businesses around the world. Some attacks have moved from initial targeting to powerful administrator-level access in under three hours. That leaves companies very little time to recognize an attack and stop it. If hackers reach a business that stores your personal information, you could end up dealing with the consequences. Here's how ARTEX works, why the FBI is concerned and what you can do to protect yourself. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS What is the ARTEX AI hacking tool? ARTEX started as a legitimate penetration testing framework. Cybersecurity professionals use these tools to find weaknesses in computer systems before criminals discover them. However, hackers have found ways to turn ARTEX against organizations without permission. The framework uses artificial intelligence to handle tasks that previously required significant hacking expertise. It can search for security weaknesses and attempt to exploit them. Once inside a system, ARTEX can work toward gaining higher levels of access and extracting sensitive information. What makes ARTEX particularly concerning is its ability to operate with limited human involvement. Attackers can give the software instructions, then let AI agents carry out much of the work automatically. ARTEX also connects to external AI models, including OpenAI's GPT and Anthropic's Claude. It supports DeepSeek and several other models. These integrations allow the framework to process instructions and automate complicated hacking operations. Their availability does not mean the AI companies are directing the attacks. According to the FBI, the technology allows criminals with relatively little technical knowledge to launch sophisticated attacks against multiple organizations simultaneously. FBI warns ARTEX hackers can gain access in under 3 hours In a November 13, 2026, security advisory, the FBI warned that criminals have used ARTEX in cyberattacks since at least August 2026. The agency identified campaigns targeting financial institutions and healthcare organizations. Government agencies and technology companies have also appeared among the targets. The speed of these attacks is especially troubling. According to the FBI, some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. That means hackers obtained powerful permissions that could allow them to make changes inside compromised systems. ARTEX can also identify weaknesses in systems that companies sometimes overlook. These include employee portals and older business applications. Criminals may exploit vulnerable third-party connections to reach organizations with stronger security. Although automated attacks can trigger security alerts, their speed creates another challenge. A company's security team might detect suspicious activity only after criminals have already gained access. How hackers used ARTEX to attack Microsoft 365 One of the clearest examples involves Microsoft 365, the service millions of employees rely on for work email and company files. In October 2026, hackers exploited compromised application credentials associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup. The service, formerly known as SkyKick Cloud Backup, helps businesses back up Microsoft 365 information. Here's why that attack is so concerning. The compromised applications already had permission to access customer environments. Hackers took advantage of those existing permissions to authenticate without needing an employee to sign in. In an October 21 investigation, Microsoft attributed the campaign to a China-state-aligned hacking group it tracks as Storm-0940. The group used ARTEX to speed up its operations and attempt access to more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 customer environments. Cybersecurity company Huntress reported unauthorized sign-ins across at least 162 customer environments during its initial investigation. However, the number of environments targeted does not represent the number where criminals stole information. Microsoft specifically warned that successful authentication does not automatically mean customer data was accessed or taken. The attack also did not result from a vulnerability in Microsoft's own systems or services. Hackers exploited permissions associated with a trusted third-party application. For businesses, that's a serious concern. Employees could have strong passwords and multifactor authentication enabled, yet criminals might still gain access through a compromised application the company already trusts. ARTEX cyberattacks have already exposed personal information The Microsoft 365 incident represents only part of the FBI's warning. In South Korea, hackers used ARTEX in attacks against financial institutions. Those attacks exposed personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 people, according to the FBI. In a separate investigation, South Korean authorities arrested seven suspects connected to attacks against more than 90 organizations. Police said the group stole approximately 8.2 million data records, with ARTEX reportedly used in many of the attacks. Researchers have also identified a separate international cyberespionage campaign. Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked hacking group known as Vapor Panda used ARTEX in attacks targeting more than 200 organizations across 14 countries. The campaign compromised at least nine organizations. The AI agents helped criminals identify vulnerabilities and obtain credentials. When one attack method failed, the software could attempt another approach. These incidents show how quickly AI-assisted hacking has expanded from individual targets to coordinated attacks against organizations around the world. Why the ARTEX warning should concern you You probably have never heard of ARTEX before now. But the businesses you depend on could become targets. Think about the information your employer keeps on file. It may include your Social Security number and banking details for direct deposit. Your healthcare provider holds sensitive medical information, while financial institutions maintain records connected to your identity. If criminals steal information from those organizations, they could use it to attempt identity theft or target you with convincing scams. A hacker who obtains your email address and details about your employer could create a phishing message that looks legitimate. A message mentioning a company you actually do business with may be harder to recognize as fraudulent. There's another concern. Your personal information could be exposed through a company you barely remember giving it to. The FBI has not warned that ARTEX automatically compromises personal phones or home computers. Its advisory focuses on attacks against organizations and the systems they operate. Still, you don't have to be the direct target of a cyberattack to feel its effects. NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH Why removing ARTEX from GitHub hasn't stopped the attacks The original ARTEX developer released the framework publicly in July 2026. After reports emerged that criminals were abusing it, the developer removed the original GitHub repository on October 8. However, the software remains available through archived copies and modified versions. The FBI also identified a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles. That figure refers to accessible framework interfaces, rather than 1,600 confirmed criminal operations. Removing the original project did little to eliminate copies already circulating online. How to protect yourself from AI-powered cyberattacks While companies are responsible for securing their systems, you can still take steps to protect your personal information and limit the damage if a business you trust gets hacked. Use strong passwords and a password manager If criminals steal login credentials from one organization, they may test those credentials against other accounts. Reusing passwords makes that easier. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A reputable password manager can generate secure passwords and store them for you. Start with your primary email account because criminals who gain access to it may be able to reset passwords for other services. Turn on multifactor authentication or passkeys Multifactor authentication adds another security check when someone tries to sign in to your account. Enable it for your email and financial services whenever available. Choose a passkey or authenticator app when supported. Passkeys can provide stronger protection against phishing than traditional passwords. Keep in mind that these protections cannot prevent every attack. The ConnectWise incident involved compromised application credentials rather than someone entering an employee's password. Check which apps have access to your accounts You may have granted third-party applications permission to access your Google or Microsoft account without thinking much about it. Review those connections periodically. Remove permissions for unfamiliar services or applications you no longer need. For personal Microsoft accounts, visit account.microsoft.com. For Google accounts, review your connected apps through myaccount.google.com. Look for unfamiliar sign-ins while you're there. If something seems suspicious, secure the account and revoke any sessions you don't recognize. For work accounts, contact your IT department before changing business application permissions. Watch for suspicious breach notifications Cybercriminals often use major security incidents to create convincing phishing messages. You might receive an email claiming your bank was hacked and asking you to verify your password. Another message could direct you to a fake account recovery page. Avoid clicking unexpected links or opening unfamiliar attachments. Instead, visit the company's official website or open its app directly to check for alerts. Never share verification codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly, even if the person claims to work for your bank. Keep your devices updated and use antivirus protection Install security updates on your computer and phone. These updates frequently address vulnerabilities criminals could exploit. Strong antivirus software with real-time protection can also help identify malicious downloads and suspicious programs. Some security tools offer additional protection against phishing websites. However, antivirus software on your personal computer cannot prevent criminals from compromising a company's cloud systems. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com. Monitor your accounts for unusual activity Check your financial accounts regularly and enable transaction alerts. These notifications can help you spot unauthorized activity quickly. Review your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or credit inquiries. You can request free reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. If your Social Security number has been exposed, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A credit freeze is free and can make it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts using your identity. A freeze will not prevent fraud involving accounts that are already open, so continue monitoring those accounts. VISA, MASTERCARD AND JPMORGAN CUSTOMER DATA LEAKED Know what to do if your information is exposed If a company notifies you about a breach, find out exactly what information was compromised. Then take action based on the type of data involved. You can also report suspected internet crime to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Kurt's key takeaways A backup service is supposed to help protect a company's information. In the ConnectWise attack, hackers abused that trusted connection to gain access to customer systems. That's especially concerning because employees could have followed every security recommendation and still been exposed through a service their company depended on. The speed of these AI-powered attacks also worries me. Three hours gives security teams very little time to stop criminals who know exactly where they're going. I think companies need to take a much harder look at the outside applications they trust and how quickly they can detect unauthorized access. For you, the best approach is to secure your own accounts and pay attention when a company reports a breach. You shouldn't have to become a cybersecurity expert to feel confident that businesses are protecting your information. If AI-powered hackers can gain privileged access to company systems in less than three hours, do you still trust businesses to protect your personal information, or should companies face tougher consequences when that information gets exposed? articles.title: Army detonation of lead azide moved to Wednesday in Iowa
articles.summary: The U.S. Army announced it will detonate more than 60 barrels of lead azide later this week, following a legal battle that placed two different blocks on the planned explosion. The controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is now scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to a statement released by the Army. “While…
articles.body:
The U.S. Army announced it will detonate more than 60 barrels of lead azide later this week, following a legal battle that placed two different blocks on the planned explosion.

The controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is now scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to a statement released by the Army .

“While the detonation is a federal operation, it’s important for the state to be engaged in the preparation process so we can support the work of our federal partners in responding to the needs of Iowans,” Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) wrote in a statement shared with The Hill.

“Protecting the health and safety of our people and communities is our highest priority,” she added.

Reynolds activated Iowa’s State Emergency Operations Center on Friday, which triggered meetings with state and federal partners in advance of the planned detonation. The talks centered on gathering information and ensuring the local area was ready for the explosion.

It was previously scheduled for Nov. 20, but lawmakers bashed the Army for a lack of communication over the plan while two environmental groups sued, arguing the environmental and health risks the detonation could pose on nearby Iowans and some residents in Illinois’s Mercer County weren’t properly explored.

The Army previously stated the detonation needed to occur before a certain date, as a forecast temperature drop later this week could make the lead azide even more unstable.

One complaint filed by environmental groups alleged the detonations would release elevated levels of lead dust into the air that could extend 100 miles north of the ammunition plant, leaving it to linger in “yards, gardens, and play areas” for years to come.

Inhaling or swallowing lead is highly dangerous to animals and humans, particularly children, and can pose serious health risks, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. There are no known safe levels of exposure.

“I remain concerned about the potential health risks resulting from the U.S. Army’s planned detonation in Middletown and the lack of clear communication and transparency from the U.S. Army,” Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa) said Sunday evening .

He also called for a full probe into how the lead azide “was allowed to degrade into this critical state and why safer methods of disposal were not pursued.”

images.caption: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on November 19, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO, just more than a week after he stepped down in the face of an affair scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and…
articles.body:
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO, just more than a week after he stepped down in the face of an affair scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s board chair, said in a statement Monday.

“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company,” he continued. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.”

Huang, who led the company for more than 30 years, resigned earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair. Reports indicated he had an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believed was passing information to China.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to bring Huang back following a series of meetings with the longtime chief executive, after which they were satisfied with his “candor and ability to lead NVIDIA,” according to a press release.

The board also received input from “senior levels” of the U.S. government , saying it is confident his reinstatement poses no national security risk.

President Trump, a prominent ally of Huang, praised Nvidia’s board of directors for the decision, stating it “made the correct and proper decision.”

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Monday morning.

“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security,” Trump continued, adding that Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the U.S. government does not have evidence he engaged “in any unlawful conduct.”

Trump said last week he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated and would not say whether he thought the woman was a spy.

“I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy, and I’ve said that,” he told reporters last week. “I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy. We’ll determine that.”

images.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks during a press conference at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO summit in Gyeongju, South Korea, Oct. 31, 2025.
